papers.title: Matrices with displacement structure: a deterministic approach for linear systems and nullspace bases
papers.abstract: For matrices with a displacement structure, the fastest known algorithms for solving linear systems and computing nullspace bases are randomized, with respective costs of $\tilde{O}(\alpha^{\omega-1} n)$ and $\tilde{O}(\alpha^2 n)$ operations in the base field. Here $n \times n$ is the matrix size, $\alpha$ is its displacement rank, $\omega > 2$ is a feasible exponent for matrix multiplication, and $\tilde{O}(\cdot)$ hides logarithmic factors. For a long time, such structured solvers were also the fastest known method to perform Hermite-Pad\'e or simultaneous Pad\'e approximations, and their interpolation variants, until recently when these problems received efficient and deterministic solutions via polynomial matrix algorithms. This work proposes to take the converse direction, by showing that these recent polynomial matrix tools can be used to improve structured matrix computations. We present a new approach which, for the Toeplitz-like, Vandermonde-like, and Cauchy-like structures, solves linear systems and computes nullspace bases in $\tilde{O}(\alpha^{\omega-1}(m+n))$ operations for an arbitrary $m \times n$ matrix, deterministically and with no assumption on the base field. This bound matches the best known randomized one for linear systems and improves upon it for nullspaces. The approach reformulates the problem as a modular equation on univariate polynomials, and describes all its solutions in three steps: computing a basis of solutions to a vector M-Pad\'e approximation problem, solving a polynomial matrix equation to get rid of unwanted unknowns, and finding the sought unknowns via simultaneous M-Pad\'e approximation.

papers.title: Optimal Configurations for Mordell's Problem
papers.abstract: Mordell's problem asks for the largest product of squared pairwise distances among $n$ points in the complex plane with a prescribed sum of squared distances from the origin. When this sum equals $n$, the maximum for $2\le n\le5$ is known to be $n^n$, attained precisely by the $n$th roots of unity up to rotation and relabeling. For $n\ge6$, Chalk showed that a regular polygon together with its center gives a larger product than the regular $n$-gon. We prove that for $6\le n\le9$ the maximum is $(n-1)^{n-1}r_n^{n(n-1)}$, where $r_n=\sqrt{n/(n-1)}$. Up to the same symmetries, the unique maximizer consists of the origin and the vertices of a regular $(n-1)$-gon of radius $r_n$. For six points, algebraic elimination reduces the proof to an exact comparison of stationary values. For seven points, we compare all twelve classes in a published classification of equilibria. For eight and nine points, rigorous interval arithmetic establishes an inequality for every admissible pair. Summing over pairs gives the sharp global bound, and the equality conditions determine the configuration. An explicit ten-point comparison and a known instability result together exclude Chalk's configuration for every $n\ge10$. For each $n$ from two through eight, Mordell's problem and the minimum-diameter problem studied by Bateman and Erd\H{o}s have a common optimal configuration.

papers.title: Integer points close to a transcendental curve: an algorithmic approach
papers.abstract: In this article, we propose an algorithmic approach to determine the integer points located near a transcendental curve. This approach is closely related to a celebrated work by Bombieri and Pila and to the so-called Coppersmith's method. We establish the underlying theoretical foundations, prove the algorithms, study their complexity and present practical experiments; we also compare our approach with previously existing ones. From a practical point of view, we focus on an instance of our general problem, called the Table Maker's Dilemma, whose solving makes it possible to evaluate a given function with correct rounding. Our experiments show a significant speedup. In particular, our results show that the development of a correctly rounded mathematical library for the binary128 format is now possible at a much smaller cost than with previously existing approaches.

papers.title: AutoSINDy: Discovery of Nonlinear Dynamics with Automated Library Construction
papers.abstract: Discovering governing equations from observational data remains a fundamental challenge in scientific modeling, particularly when the underlying mathematical structure is unknown. Traditional sparse identification methods like SINDy excel at discovering parsimonious models but require researchers to specify candidate basis functions a priori, a limitation that often leads to model failure when critical terms are omitted. We present AutoSINDy, a hybrid Discovery-then-Solve framework that combines the exploratory power of symbolic regression with the robust sparsity-promoting capabilities of SINDy. Our method operates in three stages: (1) PySR-based symbolic regression discovers candidate functional forms from random subsets of the data; (2) a curation pipeline decomposes, expands, and filters these expressions using collinearity analysis to construct a minimal yet comprehensive library; and (3) the weak form of SINDy identifies sparse governing equations from this custom-tailored library. Extensive experiments across six canonical nonlinear systems, with noise of up to 20% of each variable's standard deviation, demonstrate that AutoSINDy achieves a recovery rate (new-trajectory R^2 > 0.99) of 89.7% across all trials, against at most 45.0% for the baselines, and 67.5% at the highest noise level. Compared with standard SINDy using enriched libraries, its weak form, and standalone symbolic regression, AutoSINDy achieves higher predictive accuracy, superior generalization to unseen trajectories, and equations close to the ground-truth complexity. These results show that AutoSINDy identifies correct governing terms without prior domain knowledge, automating the feature-engineering bottleneck in system identification and offering a pathway for discovering complex dynamics in biological and physical systems where the mathematical form is unknown.
